meta.title: Who really said "Well-behaved women rarely make history"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Marilyn Monroe. Historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich wrote it in a 1976 journal article — original word "seldom." The "rarely" line pinned on Monroe is a later variant.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Well-behaved women rarely make history'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Marilyn Monroe. Historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich coined it in 1976 (as "seldom"). The "rarely" version credited to Monroe is a later paraphrase.

answer.label: Not Marilyn Monroe — actually Laurel Thatcher Ulrich
answer.sourceLine: Marilyn Monroe never said this. The sentence was coined by historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich in a 1976 article in the journal American Quarterly — and her original wording was “seldom,” not “rarely.” The “rarely” form that later got pinned on Monroe is a paraphrase of Ulrich’s line, which she wrote about the pious, forgotten women of colonial New England, not as a feminist rallying cry.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “Vertuous Women Found: New England Ministerial Literature, 1668–1735”

source.excerpt: Well-behaved women seldom make history; against Antinomians and witches, these pious matrons have had little chance at all.
trail: 1976: Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, then a doctoral student, writes “Well-behaved women seldom make history” in American Quarterly, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1990s: the line escapes onto T-shirts, mugs and bumper stickers — a “rarely” variant appears as an epigraph in Kay Mills’s From Pocahontas to Power Suits (1995), per Wikiquote ↗.
2002 onward: the saying gets falsely credited to Marilyn Monroe (also to Eleanor Roosevelt and Anne Boleyn), a misattribution documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
2007: Ulrich publishes a book titled Well-Behaved Women Seldom Make History, cementing the correct wording and author (publisher ↗).
source.excerptNote: The opening of Ulrich’s 1976 article. She was describing ordinary, devout women praised in Puritan funeral sermons — women overlooked precisely because they were dutiful. It was a call for better history, not a slogan urging women to misbehave.
source.rightsHolder: Laurel Thatcher Ulrich; originally published in American Quarterly (Johns Hopkins University Press)
source.rightsNote: The sentence originates in Ulrich’s 1976 American Quarterly article and her 2007 book of the same title — both well after 1931, so the phrase is in copyright to the author and her publishers. The popular “rarely” wording is a later paraphrase, not a public-domain text.

author.name: Laurel Thatcher Ulrich
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: b. 1938 · American historian · Harvard University · Pulitzer Prize winner
author.bio: Laurel Thatcher Ulrich is an American historian of early America and women’s history, later a professor at Harvard. She won the 1991 Pulitzer Prize for History for A Midwife’s Tale. She coined “well-behaved women seldom make history” in a 1976 scholarly article — and has said she was bemused to watch the line become a pop-culture slogan detached from her name.

misattribution.heading: How Marilyn got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s cleaner cases of a real, traceable author being displaced by a famous face. The wording was also altered along the way.

items.why: There is no source in which Monroe says or writes this line; the Monroe credit surfaces around 2002, decades after Ulrich coined it, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The saying has also been pinned on Eleanor Roosevelt and Anne Boleyn in circulation, none supported by any primary source (Quote Investigator ↗).

Ulrich wrote “seldom.” The “rarely” (and sometimes “never”) versions are later paraphrases that spread on merchandise and social media; a “rarely” epigraph appears as early as Kay Mills’s 1995 book, per Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The real line is Laurel Thatcher Ulrich’s, written as “Well-behaved women seldom make history” in American Quarterly in 1976 — not Monroe’s, and not with “rarely” (source ↗).

context.heading: What she actually meant
lead: Ulrich’s point was the opposite of the slogan it became. Studying Puritan funeral sermons, she noticed that the women praised in them — quiet, dutiful, pious — left almost no trace in the historical record precisely because they conformed. Her sentence was a lament that conventional history overlooks ordinary women, and a challenge to historians to recover their lives.

On T-shirts and mugs the line flipped into a cheeky call to misbehave. Ulrich has written wryly about watching her scholarly aside take on this second, unintended life — and about how easily it shed her name for a more marketable one.
context.pull: She was mourning the women history forgot — not telling anyone to cause trouble.
